sections.name: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR

requirement.label: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
requirement.notes: Note: The following courses will NOT apply to the major: Math 100A-B, 193, 195A-B; PSTAT 109, 188, 190, 193.

sections.notes:
With an advisor’s approval, 4 of the 52 UD units may be non-mathematics courses taken as part of a coherent
mathematics program.

narrative: To be admitted to full major status, students must complete the following pre-major Mathematics courses with a UC grade-point average of 2.5 or higher. All pre-major courses must be completed with a grade of “C” or better. Preparation courses are excluded from the pre-major GPA, but will apply to the overall major GPA. Entry into the pre-major does not guarantee admission to full major status. While completing required preparation, students are classified as pre-majors.

MAJOR REGULATIONSPREREQUISITES Check the General Catalog for the prerequisites to all listed courses.
P/NP GRADING OPTION Not allowed for major courses (prep or UD major), including courses applied to the major from other departments.
SUBSTITUTIONS In the major requirements permissible only by petition to the department chair and dean.
G.P.A REQUIREMENTS At least 2.0 overall UC average in all upper-division major courses and all courses (Prep and UD) for the major.
DOUBLE MAJORS With the approval of each department chairperson, up to a total of 8 units may be applied simultaneously to both UD majors.

nodes.title: Introduction to Computer Science
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Computer Programming
nodes.description: Introduction to computer program development for students with little to no programming experience. Basic programming concepts, variables and expressions, data and control structures, algorithms, debugging, program design, and documentation.

nodes.title: Intermediate Python Programming
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Computer Programming
nodes.prereq_text: CMPSC 8 or CMPSC W8 or ENGR 3 or ENGR W3 or ECE 3 with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Intermediate topics in Computer Science using the Python programming language. Topics include object oriented programming, runtime analysis, data structures, and software testing methodologies.

nodes.title: Problem Solving with Computers I
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Computer Programming
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 3A or 2A with a grade of C or better (may be taken concurrently), CS 8 or Engineering 3 or ECE 3 with a grade of C or better, or significant prior programming experience.
nodes.description: Fundamental building blocks for solving problems using computers. Topics include basic computer organization and programming constructs: memory CPU, binary arithmetic, variables, expressions, statements, conditionals, iteration, functions, parameters, recursion, primitive and composite data types, and basic operating system and debugging tools.

nodes.title: Problem Solving with Computers II
nodes.prereq_text: Computer Science 16 with a grade of C or better; and Mathematics 3B or 2B with a grade of C or better (may be taken concurrently).
nodes.description: Intermediate building blocks for solving problems using computers. Topics include intermediate object-oriented programming, data structures, object-oriented design, algorithms for manipulating these data structures and their run-time analyses. Data structures introduced include stacks, queues, lists, trees, and sets.

nodes.title: Data Programming and Analytics for Artificial Intelligence
nodes.prereq_text: CMPSC 9 or CMPSC 24 with a grade of C or better; and, Mathematics 3A or 2A with a grade of C or better (may be taken concurrently).
nodes.description: Course delves into essential programming, algorithmic, and data analytics techniques foundational to artificial intelligence. Topics include data acquisition, cleaning, transformation, modeling, sampling, visualization and simulation, statistical programming, hypothesis testing, inference, with applications in artificial intelligence. Students will apply these concepts through hands-on Python projects, gaining practical experience in using data analytics to develop intelligent systems.

nodes.title: Foundations of Computer Science
nodes.prereq_text: Computer Science 16 with a grade of C or better and Mathematics 4A with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Introduction to the theoretical underpinnings of computer science. Topics include propositional predicate logic, set theory, functions and relations, counting, mathematical induction and recursion (generating functions).

nodes.title: Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science
nodes.prereq_text: Computer Science 16 with a grade of C or better and Mathematics 4A with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Introductory discrete mathematics. Topics include fundamental principles of counting (permutations, combinations), sets, graph theory, elementary probability, and number theory.

nodes.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
nodes.prereq_text: CMPSC 40 or CMPSC 41 or MATH 8 with a grade of C or better; CMPSC 24 or CMPSC 25 with a grade of C or better; PSTAT 120A or ECE 139 (may be taken concurrently with CMPSC 130A); open to Computer Science Department majors, and Electrical and Computer Engineering Department majors only.

items.text: open to Computer Science Department majors, and Electrical and Computer Engineering Department majors only

nodes.description: Data structures and applications with proofs of correctness and analysis. Hash Tables, Priority Queues (heaps); Balanced Search Trees. Graph Traversal techniques and their applications.

nodes.title: Machine Learning
nodes.prereq_text: Computer Science 130A.
nodes.description: Covers the most important techniques of machine learning (ML) and includes discussions of: well-posed learning problems; artificial neural networks; concept learning and general to specific ordering; decision tree learning; genetic algorithms; Bayesian learning; analytical learning; and others.

nodes.title: Introduction to Computer Science
nodes.description: Introduction to computer program development for students with little to no programming experience. Basic programming concepts, variables and expressions, data and control structures, algorithms, debugging, program design, and documentation.

nodes.title: Introduction to Python Programming For Engineers
nodes.prereq_text: Open to EE and CMPEN majors only.

requires.text: Open to EE and CMPEN majors only

nodes.description: This course represents a comprehensive foundation for core ECE topics in signal processing, image analysis, machine learning, optimization and control. The lectures present concepts from linear algebra, such as matrix computations, systems of linear equations, eigenspace decomposition, inner-product, orthogonality, least-squares and linear regression. Students actively engage with the technical materials with an introduction to Python programming and associated hands-on sessions. The materials are be motivated by real-world scenarios ranging from medical imaging to autonomous vehicles, from (miscarriage of) justice to brain-machine interfaces, from music analysis to GPS design.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: Open to Electrical Engineering, Computer Engineering and pre-Computer Engineering majors only.

requires.text: Open to Electrical Engineering, Computer Engineering and pre-Computer Engineering majors only

nodes.description: Fundamentals of probability, conditional probability, Bayes rule, random variables, functions of random variables, expectation and high-order moments, Markov chains, hypothesis testing.

nodes.title: Introduction to Programming
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Computer Programming
nodes.description: General philosophy of programming and problem-solving. Students will be introduced to the programming language MATLAB. Specific areas of study will include algorithms, basic decision structures, arrays, matrices, and graphing.

nodes.title: Introduction to Programming
nodes.description: General philosophy of programming and problem-solving. Students will be introduced to the programming language MATLAB. Specific areas of study will include algorithms, basic decision structures, arrays, matrices, and graphing.

nodes.title: Calculus with Algebra and Trigonometry
nodes.prereq_text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam.

requires.text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam

nodes.description: Math 3A with precalculus: A function approach integrating algebra, trigonometry, and differential calculus. Topics include: one-on-one and onto functions; inverse functions; properties and graphs of polynomial, rational, exponential, and logarithmic functions; properties and graphs of trigonometric functions; analytic geometry; functions and limits; derivatives; techniques and applications of differentiation; introduction to integration; logarithmic and trigonometric functions.

nodes.title: Calculus with Algebra and Trigonometry
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Math 3B with precalculus: A continued review of relevant topics from precalculus (see Math 2A); integral calculus, including definite and indefinite integrals; techniques of integration, introduction to sequences and series; with applications in mathematics and physics.

nodes.title: Calculus with Applications, First Course
nodes.prereq_text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam.

requires.text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam

nodes.description: Differential Calculus including analytic geometry, functions and limits, derivatives, techniques and applications of differentiation; introduction to integration; logarithmic and trigonometric functions.

nodes.title: Calculus with Applications, Second Course
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 3A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Integral calculus including definite and indefinite integrals, techniques of integration; introduction to sequences and series; with applications in mathematics and physics.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra with Applications
groups: PRE-MAJOR: Linear Algebra and Differential Equations
nodes.prereq_text: Math 2B or 3B or 3BI with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Systems of linear equations, matrix algebra, determinants, vector spaces and subspaces, basis and dimension, linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, and orthogonality.

nodes.title: Differential Equations
groups: PRE-MAJOR: Linear Algebra and Differential Equations
nodes.prereq_text: Math 4A or Math 4AI with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: First and second order differential equations, separation of variables, linear differential equations, systems of first order equations, nonlinear differential equations and stability.

nodes.title: Vector Calculus with Applications, First Course
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4A (or 4AI) with a letter grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Calculus of functions of several variables, vector valued functions of one variable, derivative and integrals of vector functions, double and triple integrals, properties and applications of integrals, change of variables.

nodes.title: Vector calculus with Applications, Second Course
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4B (or 4BI) and Mathematics 6A, each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Scalar and vector fields, integration along paths, integration over surfaces and solid regions, integral theorems of vector calculus, Fourier series, partial differential equations.

nodes.title: Transition to Higher Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4A or 4AI or 4B or 4BI or 6A or 6B with a grade of B or better.
nodes.description: Introduction to the elements of propositional logic, techniques of mathematical proof, and fundamental mathematical structures, including sets, functions, relations, and other topics as time permits. Mastery of this material is essential for students planning to major in mathematics.

nodes.title: Calculus for Social and Life Sciences
nodes.description: Introduction to differential and integral calculus with applications to modeling in the biological sciences.

nodes.title: Group Studies in Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4A or 4AI or 4B or 4BI or 6A or 6B with a grade of B or better.
nodes.description: Lectures and discussions on special topics. Designed for transfer students only.

nodes.title: Classical Number Systems
nodes.prereq_text: Math 8 with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: A development of classical number systems starting with natural numbers and progressing through the integral, rational, real and complex number systems. Includes an introduction to number theory, mathematical induction, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic and the Euclidean algorithm. Especially suitable for prospective middle and high school teachers.

nodes.title: Mathematical Systems
nodes.prereq_text: Math 101A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: The theory of operations within rings and fields. Polynomials, the fundamental theorem of algebra and other factorization theorems. Analyzing linear, polynomial, rational and exponential functions. Solving algebraic equations and inequalities. Especially suitable for prospective middle and high school teachers.

nodes.title: Modern Euclidean and Noneuclidean Geometry
nodes.prereq_text: Math 8 with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Topics in plane and solid geometry. The axioms of pure, euclidean, projective, and noneuclidean geometry. Transformational geometry (isometries, dilitations, involutions, perspectivities, and projectivities). The history and the historical implications of these developments in geometry. Especially suitable for prospective middle and high school teachers.

nodes.title: Modern Euclidean and Noneuclidean Geometry
nodes.prereq_text: Math 102A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Topics in plane and solid geometry. The axioms of pure, euclidean, projective, and noneuclidean geometry. Transformational geometry (isometries, dilitations, involutions, perspectivities, and projectivities). The history and the historical implications of these developments in geometry. Especially suitable for prospective middle and high school teachers.

nodes.title: Introduction Into Numerical Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4B or 4BI, 6A, and 6B; and, Math 8 or PSTAT 8, and Math 117 and, Computer Science 5AA-ZZ or 10 or 8 or 16 or Engineering 3, each with a grade of C or above.
nodes.description: Numerical methods for the solution of nonlinear equations (Newton method), for integration (quadrature formulas and composite integration), and for the initial value problem for ordinary differential equations (Euler and Kutta methods).

nodes.title: Numerical Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: Math 104A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Numerical methods for the solution of systems of linear equations (direct and iteractive methods), and the finite difference methods for boundary value problems for (ordinary and partial) differential equations.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics in Numerical Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: Math 104B with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Topics in approximation theory; numerical methods for finding eigenvalues of a matrix; and advanced topics in numerical methods for ordinary and partial differential equations.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 4A and 8 each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Abstract vector spaces and subspaces. Span and linear independence. Basis and dimension. Linear maps. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 108A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Diagonalization, inner product spaces, projections, least-squares approximations, invariant factors and elementary divisors, canonical forms, topics from advanced matrix theory, applied linear algebra, and group representation theory.

nodes.title: Matrix Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: Math 108A with a minimum grade of C
nodes.description: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors and similarity; Unitary equivalence and normal matrices; QR factorization; Least squares; Singular Value decomposition; Moore-Penrose generalized inverse; Hermitian and symmetric matrices; Variational characterization of eigenvalues; Positive definite matrices; Nonnegative matrices; Perron-Frobenius Theorem.

nodes.title: Abstract Algebra
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 108A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: An introduction to group theory, focusing on finite groups. Basic algebraic concepts including homomorphisms, normal subgroups, quotients, direct products and group actions. Classification of finitely generated Abelian groups. Other topics such as semidirect products and Sylow theorems as time permits.

nodes.title: Abstract Algebra
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 111A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Ring theory, ideals, factorization. Examples include number rings and polynomial rings. Module theory if time permits.

nodes.title: Abstract Algebra
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 111B with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Fields, field extensions, Galois theory.

nodes.title: Non-euclidean Geometry
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 8 with a grade of "C" or better.
nodes.description: An introduction to hyperbolic geometry with some discussion of other non-euclidean systems.

nodes.title: Introduction to Number Theory
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 8 with a grade of "C" or better.
nodes.description: Number-theoretic functions, divisibility, congruences, primitive roots and indices, quadratic residues and the quadratic reciprocity law.

nodes.title: Introduction to Number Theory
nodes.prereq_text: Math 115A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Selected topics at the discretion of the instructor. Possibilities include (but are not limited to) Diophantine equations, the distribution of primes, number-theoretic methods in cryptography, quadratic forms, continued fractions, algebraic number theory, and partitions.

nodes.title: Combinatorial Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 8 with a grade of "C" or better.
nodes.description: Elementary counting principles, binomial coefficients, generating functions, recurrence relations, the principle of inclusion and exclusion, distributions and partitions, systems of distinct representatives, applications to computation.

nodes.title: Methods of Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 8 or PSTAT 8 with a grade of "C" or better.
nodes.description: Introduction to methods of proof in analysis. topics include limits, sequences and series, continuity, compactness, as well as other topics. This course is intended to follow Mathematics 8 and to introduce students to the level of sophistication of upper-division mathematics.

nodes.title: Real Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 4B, 6A, 108A and 117, each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Axioms of the real numbers, topology of metric spaces, numerical sequences, infinite series.

nodes.title: Real Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 108B and 118A, each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Real functions: continuity, differentiability, Riemann integrals, power and trigonometric series.

nodes.title: Real Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 118B with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Multivariable calculus and a selection of other topics including differential forms or Lebesgue integral.

nodes.title: Ordinary Differential Equations
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4B or 4BI and 6A with a minimum grade of C; and Math 8 with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Existence, uniqueness, and stability; the geometry of phase space; linear systems and hyperbolicity; maps and diffeomorphisms.

nodes.title: Chaotic Dynamics and Bifurcation Theory
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 6B and Math 119A, each with a minimum grade of C
nodes.description: Hyperbolic structure and chaos; center manifolds; bifurcation theory; and the Feigenbaum and Ruelle-Takens cascades to strange attractors.

nodes.title: Theory of Complex Variables
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 6A and 8 each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Complex numbers, complex differentiation, analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations, Taylor and Laurent series, classification of singular points, residues, evaluation of improper integrals.

nodes.title: Theory of Complex Variables
nodes.prereq_text: Math 122A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: The argument principle, Rouche’s theorem, analytic continuation, conformal mapping, fractional transformations and applications, infinite products, harmonic functions. Other topics at the discretion of the instructor.

nodes.title: Partial Differential Equations
nodes.prereq_text: Math 4B or 4BI, 6A, and 6B with a minimum grade of C; and Math 8 with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Introduces the derivation and solution of the fundamental linear partial differential equations (PDEs): the wave equation, the heat equation and the Laplace equation. These represent, respectively, hyperbolic, parabolic and elliptic PDEs. Focuses on first and second order PDEs. Students will master methods for initial value problems (IVPs) and boundary value problems (BVPs), including the method of characteristics and the foundational techniques of the Fourier transform and potential theory, providing a rigorous basis for understanding dynamic and steady-state physical systems.

nodes.title: Fourier Series and Numerical Methods for PDEs
nodes.prereq_text: Math 4B or 4BI, and 6A, and 6B with a minimum grade of C; and 124A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Introduces specific solution techniques used to solve the wave, heat and Laplace equations. Focuses on separation of variables, namely Fourier series, and a variety of numerical methods. Provides students with modern methods, harmonic analysis and numerical analysis, necessary to study and solve PDEs in a variety of applications. The fast Fourier transform is studied as well as finite difference methods for parabolic and elliptic PDEs and the finite element method for elliptic boundary value problems.

nodes.title: Optimization
nodes.prereq_text: Math 6A and 108A, each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Global and local optimization, constrained and unconstrained optimization, convex versus nonconvex optimization, Projection Theorem, linear search methods, gradient methods, Newton and Quasi-Newton methods, trust region methods.

nodes.title: Operations Research
nodes.prereq_text: Math 132A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Large scale optimization, stochastic gradient descent, inexact Newton methods, limited memory BSGF, least squares problems, global optimization, optimization in general normed spaces.

nodes.title: Graph and Network Theory
nodes.prereq_text: Math 4A and 8, each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Elements of graph and network theory including paths, circuits, trees, coloring, planarity, matching theory, Hall's theorem, applications to scheduling theory, flows in networks, Menger's theorem, and other topics as time permits.

nodes.title: Spectral Graph Theory
nodes.prereq_text: Math 108A and 137A, each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: The graph Laplacian, eigenvalues of weighted graphs and random walks, the normalized Laplacian and Cheegers inequality, diameters and eigenvalues, expander graphs, eigenvalues of symmetric graphs, heat kernels.

nodes.title: Introduction to Topology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 8 with a C or better. Either Math 108A or Math 117 with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Metric spaces, continuity, compactness, classification of surfaces, Euler characteristics, and fundamental groups. Additional topics at the discretion of the instructor.

nodes.title: Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: 52 UD units are required, at least 40 of which must be in Mathematics. These units must be distributed as follows.
nodes.prereq_text: Math 6A with a minimum grade of C; and Math 108A or 117 with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Curves and surfaces in three-dimensional Euclidean space, including Frenet formulas, signed curvature of plane curves, first and second fundamental forms, normal curvature and principal curvature, Gaussian and mean curvature, Gauss equation and Theorema Egregium, and a brief introduction to geodesics if time permits.

nodes.title: Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces
nodes.prereq_text: Math 6B and Math 147A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Parallel transport, geodesics, Gauss-Bonnet Theorem, fundamental theorem of surfaces. Additional topics at the discretion of the instructor may include minimal surfaces, Codazzi equation, surfaces of constant Gaussian curvature, isothermal coordinates, and global theorems for curves.

nodes.title: Introduction to Mathematical Finance
nodes.prereq_text: MATH 4B, PSTAT 120A-B, and PSTAT 160A, all completed with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Describes mathematical methods for estimating and evaluating asset pricing models, equilibrium and derivative pricing, options, bonds, and the term-structure of interest rates. Also introduces finance optimization models for risk management and financial engineering.

nodes.title: History of Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 8 with a grade of "C" or better.
nodes.description: An examination of the major achievements in mathematical thinking throughout history. Topics may include the history of numerical systems in early civilizations, the development of formal proof, mathematical contributions from diverse populations and the impact of technological innovations on mathematics. Especially suitable for prospective middle and high school teachers.

nodes.title: Special Topics in Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Math 8 with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: An advanced treatment of mathematics content appropriate for undergraduates. The material for the course may come from algebra, geometry, analysis, applied mathematics or other areas of mathematics. Topics vary by instructor.

nodes.title: Mathematical Reasonings of AI such as GPT and DeepSeek
nodes.prereq_text: Math 8 with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: This project-based course explores the mathematical reasonings of AI systems like GPT and DeepSeek. Students will work on exercises drawn from topics in Math 8, linear algebra, and calculus. For each project, the student will obtain an AI-generated solution, carefully examine it for errors, and then analyze and correct the AI's mistakes. Students will submit all project materials. Most projects will be provided by the instructor, but students will also be encouraged to find some on their own, with all projects receiving necessary instruction.

nodes.title: Problem Solving
nodes.prereq_text: Math 8 with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: The Problem Solving in Mathematics course is designed to impart students with advanced problem-solving techniques and strategies in mathematics. Students will explore a diverse range of methods, including the application of parity, coloring, ordering, extremality, symmetry, invariants among others. The course emphasizes critical and creative thinking, allowing students to tackle complex mathematical challenges. Through collaboration and presentation exercises, students develop effective communication skills. The goal is to equip students with the basic abilities for research in mathematics.

nodes.title: Mathematics Transition for Transfer Students
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4A or 4AI or 4B or 4BI or 6A or 6B with a grade of B or better. Concurrent enrollment in Math 94.
nodes.description: Provides transfer students with a solid mathematical foundation to ease their transition into a four-year college environment. Students will explore the fundamental axioms of integers and their properties, gaining a deep understanding of this essential mathematical concept. The curriculum extends to the study of rational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers, emphasizing the properties and principles that underlie these numeric systems. Through a structured approach, this course equips transfer students with the mathematical knowledge and skills necessary to excel in more advanced coursework.

nodes.title: Internship in Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Consent of instructor and department.
nodes.description: Faculty sponsored academic internship in industrial or research firms.

nodes.title: Senior Thesis
nodes.prereq_text: Open to senior majors only; consent of department and instructor.
nodes.description: Independent research under the supervision of a faculty member which will result in a senior thesis. Student will concentrate on reading and gathering material for a thesis.

nodes.title: Senior Thesis
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 197A. Open to senior majors only; consent of department and instructor.
nodes.description: Independent research under the supervision of a faculty member which will result in a senior thesis. Student will concentrate on writing a thesis.

nodes.title: Independent Studies in Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in math; consent of instructor and department.

items.text: completion of 2 upper-division courses in math

nodes.description: Coursework consists of academic research supervised by a faculty member on a topic not available in established course offerings.

nodes.title: Independent Research Assistance
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in math; consent of instructor and department.

items.text: completion of 2 upper-division courses in math

nodes.description: Coursework consists of faculty supervised research assistance.

nodes.title: Basic Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A or 3A or AP Math AB Exam with a score of 3 or better.

items.text: AP Math AB Exam with a score of 3 or better

nodes.description: Introduction to classical mechanics for students in engineering and the physical sciences. Measurement, units, and foundations of physics; vectors; kinematics; circular motion; forces, mass, and Newton's laws; center of mass; momentum; work and energy; conservation laws; collisions; rotational kinematics.

nodes.title: Introductory Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A or 3A or 34A (may be taken concurrently) or AP Math AB Exam score of 3 or better.

items.text: AP Math AB Exam score of 3 or better

nodes.description: Presents concepts and methodologies for understanding physical phenomena, and is particularly useful preparation for upper-division study in the life sciences. Vectors, velocity, acceleration. Newton's laws. Work and energy. Linear momentum. Gravity. Static equilibrium. Rotational motion. Angular momentum.

nodes.title: Basic Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A or 3A or AP Math AB Exam with a score of 3 or better.

items.text: AP Math AB Exam with a score of 3 or better

nodes.description: Kinematics in 3D, Newton’s Laws, Energy, Momentum and Collisions, Rotation, Statics and Equilibrium

nodes.title: Introduction to Mathematical Methods for Physics
nodes.description: Single variable functions, derivatives and integrals with applications to kinematics. Taylor series. Introduction to ordinary differential equations and Newtons second law as an ODE. Vectors and scalars with physics applications. Dot and cross products. Matrices and determinants. Unit circle and trigonometric identities. Polar coordinates and kinematics in polar coordinates.

nodes.title: General Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A/3A and Mathematics 2B/3B or Physics 8 or AP Calculus BC Exam score of 5.

items.text: AP Calculus BC Exam score of 5

nodes.description: Classical mechanics, kinematics, vectors, Newtons laws, work and energy, conservation laws, rotational kinematics.

nodes.title: Transition to Data Science, Probability and Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 3C or 3CI or 4A or 4AI or 4B or 4BI or 5A or 5AI or 5B or 5BI or 5C or 6A or 6AI or 6B with a grade of B or better. Not open to students who have completed Math 8.

items.text: open to students who have completed MATH 8

nodes.description: Introduction to techniques of mathematical logic, proof, and fundamental structures in probability and statistics. The curriculum includes sets, inequalities, functions, continuity, limits, infinity, and random numbers and simulation. Applications to high-dimensional probability, data science, and statistics. Mastery of this material is essential for students continuing to all three PSTAT programs.

nodes.title: Principles of Data Science with R
nodes.prereq_text: Math 2B or 3B with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Provides a foundation for the practice of data science, with an emphasis on the statistical thinking and computer programming required to collect, prepare, and analyze data. Students will explore and implement the data science life cycle in locally relevant contexts. Using the R programming language, the course focuses on the fundamental skills of data manipulation, exploratory data analysis, and data visualization. A key component of the curriculum is learning to ethically communicate findings and to consider the broader impacts of data-driven decisions.

nodes.title: Data Science Concepts and Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 120A; CS 9 or CS 16; and Math 4A, all with letter grade C or better.
nodes.description: Overview of data science key concepts and the use of tools for data retrieval, analysis, visualization, and reproducible research in preparation for advanced data science courses. Topics include an introduction to inference and prediction, principles of measurement, missing data, and notions of causality, statistical traps, and concepts in data ethics and privacy.

nodes.title: Introduction to Nonparametric Methods
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 120B both with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Statistical methods for model-free data analysis, including use of ranks in comparing means and assessing correlation, computer-based permutation and bootstrap calculations for significance tests and confidence intervals, estimation of lifetime survival curves. Emphasis on scientific applications.

nodes.title: Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 126 with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: An introduction to the Bayesian approach to statistical inference, its theoretical foundations and comparison to classical methods. Topics include parameter estimation, testing, prediction and computational methods (Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation). Emphasis on concepts, methods and data analysis. Extensive use of the R programming language and examples from the social, biological and physical sciences to illustrate concepts.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: Math 3C or Math 4A or Math 4AI or Math 6A or Math 6AI completed with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Concepts of probability; random variables; combinatorial probability; discrete and continuous distributions; joint distributions, expected values; moment generating functions; law of large numbers and central limit theorems.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 120A with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Distribution of sample mean and sample variance; t, chi-squared and F distributions; summarizing data by statistics and graphs; estimation theory for single samples: sufficiency, efficiency, consistency, methodof moments, maximum likelihood; hypothesis testing: likelihood ratio test; confidence intervals.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 120B with a grade C or better.
nodes.description: Hypothesis tests for means of independent samples and paired data; likelihood ratio tests; nonparametric hypothesis tests: sign, rank, and Mann-Whitney tests; chi-squared goodness-of-fit tests and contingency tables; Bayesian methods of estimating parameters and credible intervals.

nodes.title: Design and Analysis of Experiments
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 120B both with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: An introduction to statistical design and analysis of experiments. Covers: principles of randomization, blocking and replication; fixed, random and mixed effects models; block designs, factorial designs and nested designs; analysis of variance and multiple comparison.

nodes.title: Sampling Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 120B both with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: An elementary development of the statistical methods used to design and analyze sample surveys. Basic ideas: estimates, bias, variance, sampling and nonsampling errors; simple random sampling with and without replacement; ratio and regression estimates; stratified sampling; systematic sampling; cluster sampling; sampling with unequal probabilities, multistage sampling. Examples from various fields will be discussed to illustrate the concepts including sampling of biological populations, opinion polls, etc.

nodes.title: Regression Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 120B both with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Linear and multiple regression, analysis of residuals, transformations, variable and model selection including stepwise regression, and analysis of covariance. The course will stress the use of computer packages to solve real-world problems.

nodes.title: Advanced Statistical Models
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 126 with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Exponential family and generalized linear models including logistic and Poisson regression, nonparametric regression, including kernel, spline and local polynomials, and generalized additive models. Other topics as time allows: regularization, neural networks, and support vector machines. Emphasis will be on concepts and practical applications.

nodes.title: SAS Base Programming
nodes.prereq_text: One upper division course in PSTAT, MATH, Computer Science or ECE.

requires.text: One upper division course in PSTAT

nodes.description: In depth SAS programming course. Topics include importing/exporting raw data files, manipulating/transforming data, combining SAS data sets, generating reports, handling syntax and logic errors. Provides preparation for the SAS Institute Certified Professional (Base Programming) Examination.

nodes.title: Introduction to Statistical Machine Learning
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 120A-B and PSTAT 126 with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Statistical Machine Learning is used to discover patterns and relationships in large data sets. Topics will include: data exploration, classification and regression tress, random forests, clustering and association rules. Building predictive models focusing on model selection, model comparison and performance evaluation. Emphasis will be on concepts, methods and data analysis; and students are expected to complete a significant class project, individual or team based, using real-world data.

nodes.title: Database Management for Data Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 8/MATH 8 with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Database systems concepts and architecture, data modeling by ER, relational model, Structured Query Language (SQL), functional dependencies, normalization, physical database design decisions, transaction processing concepts and theory. Introduction to the non-relational model, NoSQL and NewSQL.

nodes.title: Statistical Data Science
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 131 or PSTAT 231 or Computer Science 165B; and Computer Science 9 (preferred) or Computer Science16. A minimum letter grade of C or better must be earned in each course.
nodes.description: Applications of advanced data science tools for data retrieval, statistical analysis and machine learning, optimization, and visualization. Multiple case studies will illustrate the practical use of these tools.

nodes.title: Big Data Analytics
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 131 or PSTAT 231 or Computer Science 165B; and Computer Science 9 (preferred) or Computer Science 16. A minimum letter grade of C or better must be earned in each course.
nodes.description: Basics in distributed data storage, retrieval, processing and cloud computing. Overview of methods for analyzing big data from both high dimensional statistics and machine learning - topics chosen from penalized regression, classification/clustering, dimension reduction, random projections, kernel methods, network clustering, graph analytics, supervised and unsupervised learning among others.

nodes.title: Statistical Process Control
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 120B both with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Topics include, statistical quality control charts for mean, standard deviation, range, fraction defective, and number of defects; sampling by attributes and variables; acceptance sampling, choice of acceptable quality level, average outgoing quality limit and lot tolerance percent defective values.

nodes.title: Applied Stochastic Processes
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4A or 4AI or 5A, Mathematics 8 or PSTAT 8, and PSTAT 120A. A minimum letter grade of C or better must be earned in each course.
nodes.description: Discrete probability models. Review of discrete and continuous probability. Conditional expectations. Simulation techniques for random variables. Discrete time stochastic processes: random walks and Markov chains with applications to Monte Carlo simulation and mathematical finance. Introduction to Poisson process.

nodes.title: Applied Stochastic Processes
nodes.prereq_text: MATH 4B, PSTAT 120B, and PSTAT 160A with a grade of C or better
nodes.description: Continuous models. Continuous time stochastic processes: Poisson process, Markov chains, Renewal process, Brownian motion, including simulation of these processes. Applications to Black-Scholes model, insurance and ruin problems and related topics.

nodes.title: Introduction to Mathematical Finance
nodes.prereq_text: MATH 4B, PSTAT 120A-B, and PSTAT 160A, all completed with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Describes mathematical methods for estimating and evaluating asset pricing models, equilibrium and derivative pricing, options, bonds, and the term-structure of interest rates. Also introduces finance optimization models for risk management and financial engineering.

nodes.title: Mathematics of Fixed Income Markets
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2B or 3B with a minimum grade of C
nodes.description: Introduction to fixed Income Markets. Topics include: measurement of interest, annuities certain, varying annuities, amortization schedules, sinking funds, bonds and related securities, depreciation.

nodes.title: Actuarial Statistics I
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 120A and 171.
nodes.description: Probabilistic and deterministic contingency mathematics in life and health insurance, annuities, and pensions. Topics include: survival distributions and life tables, life insurance, life annuities, net premiums, net premium reserves.

nodes.title: Actuarial Statistics II
nodes.prereq_text: MATH 4B and PSTAT 172A.
nodes.description: Net premium reserves, multiple life functions, multiple decrement models, valuation theory for pension plans, insurance models including expenses, nonforfeiture benefits and dividends.

nodes.title: Risk Theory
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 120B with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Risk measures, individual and collective risk models, credibility theory; applications to actuarial and financial mathematics.

nodes.title: Time Series
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 120B both with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Stationary and non-stationary models, seasonal time series, ARMA models: calculation of ACF, PACF, mean and ACF estimation. Barlett's formula, model estimation: Yule-Walker estimates, ML method. identification techniques, diagnostic checking forecasting, spectral analysis, the periodogram. Current software and applications.

nodes.title: Survival Analysis
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 10 and PSTAT 120B both with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Introduces methods for analyzing time-to-event data, focusing on both concepts and applications. Topics include survival and hazard functions, life tables, Kaplan-Meier estimation, comparison of survival curves, and regression models such as the Cox proportional hazards and accelerated failure time models. Emphasis is placed on developing intuition for the methods and interpreting results. Students will gain hands-on experience with survival analysis using R.

nodes.title: Advanced Mathematical Finance
nodes.prereq_text: MATH 4B, PSTAT 160A-B, PSTAT 170; PSTAT 160B may be taken concurrently. PSTAT 160A and PSTAT 170 must be completed with a B- or higher.

items.text: PSTAT 170 must be completed with a B-

nodes.description: Advanced topics in asset pricing models, portfolio optimization, interest rate modeling and derivative pricing. Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing, Markowitz Mean-Variance Frontier, Capital Asset Pricing Theory, Monte Carlo methods and variance reduction techniques.

nodes.title: Financial Market Risk and Modeling
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 126 and PSTAT 171 both with a minimum grade of C or better, or instructor approval.
nodes.description: Modern financial markets, interest rate risk and its effect on government bonds, corporate bonds, other fixed income investments and equities. Financial market data analysis, calibration and validation. Some additional topics from among mortgage-backed securities, corporate credit risk, inflation-indexed bonds and swaptions.

nodes.title: Tutorial in Actuarial Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: Statistics 120A
nodes.description: Problem solving sessions to prepare students for the first four actuarial examinations. Topics corresponding to these examinations (probability, financial mathematics, statistical modeling, and risk management) will be offered in different quarters.

nodes.title: Fundamental Actuarial Concepts
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 171
nodes.description: Introduces students to practical actuarial concepts and principles related to Property/Casualty Insurance (also known as General Insurance). Topics include pricing methods, reserving methods, insurance accounting, actuarial standards, and other subject matter students are likely to encounter early in their actuarial career. Examples expose students to Property Casualty Insurance; however, many of the concepts covered such as; frequency, severity, development, trend, deductibles and coinsurance, also apply to other practice areas (e.g., Life, Health, or Retirement).

nodes.title: Transfer Exploration Seminar: Statistics and Data Science
nodes.prereq_text: New transfer students only; department approval required to finalize registration.
nodes.description: Introduces students to foundational programming concepts for data analysis and visualization and fundamental concepts in probability and mathematics (random variables, set theory, simulations, series and integration), serving as preparation for follow-up major gateway courses in PSTAT. The material is organized into distinct modules and includes a brief introduction to R, Python, tidy data framework, data science ethics, and exploratory data analysis. Students will also explore research areas in the discipline, departmental and campus study resources, undergraduate research opportunities, and diverse career tracks available to Statistics & Data Science graduates.

nodes.title: Teaching and Mentoring Statistics and Data Science
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; and consent of the instructor. Minimum GPA of 3.0. Training course for Undergraduate Learning Assistant (ULA) Program. May not be applied towards major.
nodes.description: Introduction to pedagogy in probabilty and statistics. Approaches to tutoring and mentoring undergraduate students. Course includes hands-on experience working one-on-one with students during discussion sections and open lab hours in an assigned PSTAT course.

nodes.title: Internship in Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing and consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Faculty sponsored academic internship in industrial or research firms. A seven to ten page written report is required and evaluated for credit.

nodes.title: Group Studies for Advanced Students
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Lectures and discussions on special topics in probability and statistics.

nodes.title: Computational Methods in Statistics
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Using the computational power of a computer has become central to the many fields - modern statistics , data science, machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence etc. In this course students develop a working knowledge of modern computational statistics applicable to data science, machine learning, deep learning. Students will develop an understanding of how computers are used to do statistics and why these methods work. This will enable effective use of methods of computational statistics in applications. We will use R programming language.

nodes.title: Financial Market Risk and Modeling
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Modern financial markets involve a wide range of risks and investment vehicles. Understanding and modeling financial markets requires an understanding of interest rate risk andits effect on government bonds, corporate bonds, other fixed income investments and equities.

nodes.title: Transfer Exploration Seminar: Statistics & Data Science
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; consent of instructor.
nodes.description: In part I of the course, students will learn about the UCSB's approach to Statistics & Data Science and get introduced to the other Majors offered in the Department of Statistics & Applied Probability. Students will learn about PSTAT research areas and undergraduate research opportunities, and get exposed to the varied career tracks available to SDS graduates. Part II of the course will review the mathematical concepts underlying probability, foundational programming concepts in the context of exploratory data analysis & data visualization, and the data science lifecycle, targeting preparation for pre-Majors going into PSTAT 8, 10 and 120A. Course includes Labs conducted w/Python Jupyter notebooks.

nodes.title: Data Science Capstone Project Preparation
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 126; and consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Introduction to research skills. Discussion of current research trends, writing literature reviews, etc. Students will be required to present materials reflecting their interests, which will be critically appraised for both content and presentation. Emphasis will be placed on aiding students to acquire a high-level of professionalism.

nodes.title: Capstone Project in Data Science
nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 197A; and consent of the instructor. Upper-division standing only. No more than 4.0 units may be applied towards department major electives.

items.text: No more than 4.0 units may be applied towards department major electives

nodes.description: Research opportunities for undergraduate students. Students practice their data science and applied statistics skills by completing a hands-on team project on a practical problem proposed by a project sponsor. Students are expected to give regular oral presentations and prepare at least one written report on their research.

nodes.prereq_text: PSTAT 197A; PSTAT 197B; and consent of the instructor. Upper-division standing only. No more than 4.0 units may be applied toward department major electives.

nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; completion of 2 upper-division courses in PSTAT.
